question: A finance assistant's variance commentary reads well, but several of the figures quoted in it are wrong. She is about to start rewording her request. What should she do first?
options: A) Check the figures she supplied, since a commentary can only be as accurate as the numbers it was given.
B) Ask for the commentary to be produced again, this time with each figure checked as it is written out.
C) Ask for every figure in the commentary to be listed separately, so she can check them all in one place.
D) Add an instruction that accuracy of the figures matters more than the readability of the commentary.
correct_answers: A) Check the figures she supplied, since a commentary can only be as accurate as the numbers it was given.
explanations: Correct. When the reasoning and the writing are sound but the numbers are wrong, the input is the first suspect. Rewording the request cannot repair figures that were incorrect before they were pasted in.
A self-check re-reads the same numbers she supplied, so wrong inputs are confirmed rather than corrected.
A separate list makes checking easier, but it is a step she should take after establishing whether the input data was right.
Instructions about priorities do not correct an underlying number, and they invite more careful presentation of the same wrong values.
